Galatians 1.audience: Paul writes "unto the churches of Galatia" (Galatians 1:2) about teachers urging Gentile believers to be circumcised. Scholars debate whether these were the southern Galatian cities of Acts 13–14 or ethnic Galatians farther north.

culture.title: No thanksgiving
culture.text: Letters of the time usually followed the greeting with a thanksgiving, as Paul's other letters do. Galatians moves straight to "I marvel."

culture.title: Zealous for traditions
culture.text: "The traditions of my fathers" were the oral teachings the Pharisees kept alongside the written law (Mark 7:3).

culture.title: Arabia
culture.text: Arabia here likely means the Nabataean kingdom, east and south of Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32).

Galatians 2.audience: Paul describes a meeting with James, Cephas, and John in Jerusalem, and a later clash with Peter at Antioch over eating with Gentiles.

culture.title: Titus, a Greek
culture.text: Titus was an uncircumcised Gentile believer. Paul brought him to Jerusalem.

culture.title: Right hands of fellowship
culture.text: Shaking right hands sealed an agreement.

culture.title: Eating with the Gentiles
culture.text: Many Jews avoided sharing meals with Gentiles because of food laws and purity concerns (Acts 10:28; 11:3).

Galatians 3.audience: Paul asks the Galatians, "Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?" (Galatians 3:2), and argues from Abraham's story.

culture.title: Bewitched
culture.text: The word was used for the ‘evil eye,’ a curse many in the ancient world feared.

culture.title: Hanged on a tree
culture.text: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23.

culture.title: A man's covenant
culture.text: Once a will was ratified, no one could cancel it or add to it.

Galatians 4.audience: Paul reminds the Galatians how they welcomed him when he first preached to them through "infirmity of the flesh" (Galatians 4:13).

culture.title: Tutors and governors
culture.text: A wealthy child heir was under guardians and managers until the age his father set.

culture.title: Abba, Father
culture.text: Paul again uses the Aramaic word for father (Romans 8:15).

culture.title: Hagar and Sarah
culture.text: Paul draws on Genesis 16 and 21 and quotes Isaiah 54:1.

Galatians 5.audience: Paul warns against receiving circumcision and lists the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.

culture.title: Yoke of bondage
culture.text: A yoke was a wooden frame that bound animals for work, and a common image for slavery.

culture.title: A little leaven
culture.text: Paul uses the same proverb in 1 Corinthians 5:6.

culture.title: Vice and virtue lists
culture.text: Lists of vices and virtues were common in Greek moral teaching and in Jewish writings.

Galatians 6.audience: Paul ends with a note in his own hand: "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand" (Galatians 6:11).

culture.title: Large letters
culture.text: Paul usually dictated to a scribe and added a closing in his own hand (2 Thessalonians 3:17).

culture.title: The marks of the Lord Jesus
culture.text: Slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded or tattooed with their owner's or commander's mark. Paul had been stoned and beaten (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:25).

Ephesians 1.audience: Paul writes from prison (Ephesians 3:1; 4:1). Some early manuscripts lack "at Ephesus" in Ephesians 1:1, so the letter may have circulated among several churches in Asia.

culture.title: One long sentence
culture.text: In Greek these verses form a single long sentence of praise.

culture.title: Sealed
culture.text: A seal marked ownership and protected goods or documents from tampering.

culture.title: Earnest
culture.text: An earnest was a down payment guaranteeing the full amount (2 Corinthians 1:22).

Ephesians 2.audience: Paul reminds Gentile readers that they were once "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel" (Ephesians 2:12).

culture.title: The prince of the power of the air
culture.text: Many in the ancient world believed spirits lived in the air between earth and heaven.

culture.title: The middle wall of partition
culture.text: A stone barrier in the temple kept Gentiles out of the inner courts on pain of death. Paul was accused of bringing a Gentile past it (Acts 21:28–29).

culture.title: The chief corner stone
culture.text: The corner stone set the lines of a building (Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16).

Ephesians 3.audience: Paul calls himself "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" (Ephesians 3:1) and prays for the readers.

culture.title: Mystery
culture.text: Greek mystery religions kept secret rites for initiates. Paul uses the word for something once hidden but now made known.

culture.title: I bow my knees
culture.text: Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling showed special earnestness (Luke 22:41; Acts 20:36).

Ephesians 4.audience: Paul urges unity and lists gifts given to the church, quoting Psalm 68:18 (Ephesians 4:8).

culture.title: Captivity captive
culture.text: A conquering king led captives in procession and gave out gifts and spoils.

culture.title: Tossed to and fro
culture.text: Paul uses the image of a small boat thrown about by waves and wind.

culture.title: Putting off and putting on
culture.text: The picture is of changing clothes.

Ephesians 5.audience: Paul writes about walking in love and light and begins instructions for households with husbands and wives.

culture.title: Drunk with wine
culture.text: Drunkenness was a feature of the worship of Dionysus and of banquets.

culture.title: Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs
culture.text: Early Christians sang in their gatherings. Pliny wrote around AD 112 that Christians sang a hymn to Christ ‘as to a god.’

culture.title: Household codes
culture.text: Greek writers since Aristotle discussed the duties of husbands and wives, parents and children, and masters and slaves.

Ephesians 6.audience: Paul finishes the household instructions and describes "the whole armour of God." Tychicus carries the letter (Ephesians 6:21–22).

culture.title: Masters and servants
culture.text: Slaves were present in many Christian households, as both members and servants.

culture.title: A soldier's armor
culture.text: A Roman legionary wore a belt, breastplate, hobnailed sandals, a large shield, a helmet, and carried a short sword. Isaiah 59:17 describes God wearing armor of righteousness and salvation.

culture.title: An ambassador in bonds
culture.text: Ambassadors were supposed to be protected; Paul writes as one in chains.

Philippians 1.audience: Paul writes from prison (Philippians 1:13) to the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16), thanking them for their support.

culture.title: Bishops and deacons
culture.text: Paul greets overseers and helpers, the leaders of the Philippian church.

culture.title: The palace
culture.text: The palace (praetorium) was the governor's headquarters or the Praetorian Guard. Where Paul was imprisoned is debated: Rome, Ephesus, and Caesarea have all been suggested.

culture.title: Your conversation
culture.text: The Greek word means living as citizens. Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were proud of their citizenship.

Philippians 2.audience: Paul urges humility, sets out Christ's example (Philippians 2:5–11), and plans to send Timothy and Epaphroditus to them.

culture.title: The form of a servant
culture.text: Slaves had the lowest standing in society, and crucifixion was the punishment for slaves.

culture.title: Every knee should bow
culture.text: The words echo Isaiah 45:23.

culture.title: Poured out as an offering
culture.text: Wine or oil was poured out alongside a sacrifice as a drink offering (Numbers 15:5).

Philippians 3.audience: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision and lists his own background as a Hebrew and a Pharisee.

culture.title: Beware of dogs
culture.text: Dogs were scavengers in ancient cities, and the word was an insult.

culture.title: Of the tribe of Benjamin
culture.text: Benjamin gave Israel its first king, Saul, whose Hebrew name Paul shared (Acts 13:21).

culture.title: Our conversation is in heaven
culture.text: The word means citizenship or commonwealth. Philippians held Roman citizenship although they lived far from Rome.

Philippians 4.audience: Paul urges two women, Euodias and Syntyche, to agree, and thanks the church for the gifts Epaphroditus brought (Philippians 4:2, 18).

culture.title: Content in every state
culture.text: The word for content was a favorite of Stoic philosophers, who taught self-sufficiency.

culture.title: An odour of a sweet smell
culture.text: Paul describes their gift in the language of sacrifice (Leviticus 1:9).

culture.title: Caesar's household
culture.text: Caesar's household included slaves and freedmen who worked for the emperor across the empire.

Colossians 1.audience: Paul writes with Timothy to believers in Colossae, a city in the Lycus valley he had not visited (Colossians 2:1). Epaphras had brought them the gospel (Colossians 1:7).

culture.title: Colossae
culture.text: Colossae was a small city near Laodicea and Hierapolis in the province of Asia. An earthquake struck the region around AD 60–61 (Tacitus).

culture.title: Image of the invisible God
culture.text: Coins and statues carried the emperor's image throughout the empire.

culture.title: Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers
culture.text: Jewish writings of the time named ranks of angels with titles like these.

Colossians 2.audience: Paul warns against philosophy, food rules, holy days, and "worshipping of angels" (Colossians 2:8, 16, 18).

culture.title: The handwriting of ordinances
culture.text: The word was used for a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor.

culture.title: Triumphing over them
culture.text: In a Roman triumph, defeated enemies were paraded through the streets in public disgrace.

culture.title: Touch not; taste not
culture.text: Paul quotes rules being urged on them.

Colossians 3.audience: Paul calls the Colossians to "seek those things which are above" and gives household instructions.

culture.title: Barbarian, Scythian
culture.text: Scythians, nomads north of the Black Sea, were seen by Greeks as the most uncivilized of peoples.

culture.title: Bond and free
culture.text: Slaves and free people met in the same congregations.

culture.title: Household instructions
culture.text: As in Ephesians 5–6, Paul addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters.

Colossians 4.audience: Paul sends Tychicus and Onesimus with the letter (Colossians 4:7–9) and asks that it be read in Laodicea as well (Colossians 4:16).

culture.title: Seasoned with salt
culture.text: Salt was used to preserve and flavor food, and Greek writers used it of witty speech.

culture.title: Luke, the beloved physician
culture.text: This is the only place Luke's profession is named.

culture.title: The epistle from Laodicea
culture.text: Letters were copied and passed between churches. The letter from Laodicea has not survived.
